Yes, there is a file in the "code" folder called figures.py with functions to produce all the figures in the report, a function make_all_figures that runs all of them and puts them in the "figs" folder, and a main statement (i.e., via if __name__ == "__main__") that calls make_all_figures.

Due to the lack of comments, I would ordinarily have a lot of trouble figuring out exactly how I could reproduce the results. Ordinarily, I assume that I could just run figures.py and trigger the main script, but it seems more complicated than that since there is no reference to the raw dataset with the full name "/data/TBI PUD 10-08-2013.csv" in that entire file.

Fortunately, in the README, we learn the full reproducibility pipeline. The student explains that the script "will automatically pick the first CSV it finds in data/ (excluding cleaned_data.csv)", which makes sense since the original dataset is the only CSV in that subdirectory. That's why I was unable to find any reference to the full filename of the dataset.

Next, accoding to the pipeline, we can execute the bash script in run.sh, which sets up the Conda environment, reads that original dataset and uses clean_data in clean.py to generate cleaned_data.csv, which it turn uses to run models.py and figures.py. Recall that main script I mentioned in figures.py. While it doesn't mention the full name of the dataset, it does use an argument "clean_csv" as a Path object. And in the run.sh script, when figures.py is run, the argument clean_csv is set to ${CLEANED_CSV} on line 135, which is a bash variable set to cleaned_data.csv on line 24. Thus, in short, while it's not entirely clear at first glance, I think it's easy to reproduce the figures and results in the report by executing run.sh.

It's a bit hard for me to understand due to the sparsity of comments, but there are over two dozen functions in clean.py that are run together in a function called clean_pipeline. Then, as the Lab 1 instructions mandate, there is a function called clean_data that takes the path to the raw CSV as well as a few other parameters and runs clean_pipeline to generate the aforementioned a clean datafrae. Then, in the if __name__ == "__main__" statement, the raw CSV filepath is set to "data/TBI PUD 10-08-2013.csv", clean_data is called to generate df_clean (a cleaned dataframe), and some details of the execution are printed.

But I'm a bit confused since, in run.sh, we see very similar code that also generates df_clean. However, unlike the code in clean.py, run.sh not only generates df_clean but writes it to a CSV, namely cleaned_data.csv as we expect. Thus, while it wouldn't be difficult for me to use their code to clean the data how they did since I could simply execute run.sh and generate all these steps, I think it would be better for reproducibility if I could just run clean_data or the full clean.py file to generate cleaned_data.csv. Currently, running that function or file would, at least based on my reading, only give me a cleaned dataframe rather than the full cleaned CSV, but this isn't that big of an issue since it isn't hard to write it to a CSV as they themselves do in run.sh. On that note, to answer the second question, there is indeed an easy-to-use function in a separate file and it would be clean_data.

The report is a bit formulaic but mostly clear and readable. I couldn't identify any blatant grammar mistakes. But there were some points that confused me. For instance, when discussing data cleaning on page 5, the student writes the following:
"After cleaning, the final dataset has 42,412 observations and 376 ciTBI cases (0.9%), matching the published cohort size."

As they wrote, this does match one of the cohort sizes in the paper, namely the 42,412 patients with GCS scores of 14 or 15. And in their data cleaning steps, the only time they wrote that they excluded any observations is in step 1:
"We excluded records that did not match the target cohort (low GCS) and records without a ciTBI label (Figure 2B)."

But this is exactly how, in Kuppermann et al., they get from 43,399 to 42,412 observations. I think it would be a lot clearer if they just said that they're mimicking the steps in the paper, as it feels like they are purporting to take a more original data cleaning step than they actually are.

Moreover, in the reality check, they treat the fact that both their cleaned dataset and Kuppermann et al. had 42,412 observations as a reassuring sign:
"Our analytic cohort has 42,412 encounters and 376 ciTBI events (~0.9%), matching the headline numbers in the paper. We also recomputed ciTBI from its component outcomes and found no mismatches with the provided ciTBI label. Overall, these checks suggest the cleaning pipeline did not materially change the cohort or outcome."

I don't mean to be harsh and I could be misunderstanding, but this is very confusing to me since it seems trivial that their numbers and the paper's numbers are the same since they take the identical steps when it came to removing observations. In the instructions, the point of the reality check is to consider the assumptions you made during preprocessing and see how they match up to your domain knowledge, which this section doesn't do. I know this isn't exactly a point against readability, but things that like this felt out-of-place did throw me off a lot when reading the report.

As for the data exploration and findings sections, I'll admit that a lot of the methods they used confused me a bit, but that might just be my own lack of familiarity with them. It was interesting that they looked at how much the log loss changed when permuting certain features as a measure of importance.

The data cleaning was described clearly, but there could have been more detail about which steps they took and why. They also didn't provide any figures or visualizations to showcase the issues in the data that they were trying to fix. As an example of detail, they could have mentioned that the number 92 was a consistent numeric code for missing or NA, but they just refer to "numeric codes". That's not the biggest deal, but I think adding that kind of detail is important.

As for inconsistencies they missed, it's not exactly an inconsistency, but there is a lot of dependency and correlation between many columns such as the findings. They do address parent-child inconsistencies, but they don't consider whether to drop certain correlated features to avoid collinearity. They also did not address the typing issues with the data, namely how many categorical variables (48) are coded as floats. And while they address missingness elsewhere in the report, it would be helpful if they explained why they didn't drop any of the highly missing features like ethnicity and dizziness in data cleaning.

Yes, the non-findings figures are mostly relevant and discussed, but some are not sufficiently explained. The age and mechanism severity figures in Data do give a feel for the data. But I wouldn't have included the missingness figure in the Data Collection section. It makes more sense to put in Data Cleaning or Data Exploration as motivation for why we did or did not remove missing data or just a better understanding of the data. In Data Exploration, I don't think all the figures need to be about the rates of ciTBI prevalence based on age or age and mechanism severity. The template says to give us a feel for the data at a basic level, and there are so many other things to look at such as correlation between different variables or the distribution of different, non-outcome variables based on age. That's not to say that the given figures are "bad" or wrong, but it would make more sense to give a much broader view of the data in this section.

Even if it seems trivial, it would be good to label the x-axes as "Hematoma Presence" and "Reference Subgroup" for F3A and F3B, respectively. Having no x-labels just looks really off. There's also no reason to have "pp" after all the y-axis numbers since the y-axis itself is labeled Risk difference (percentage points), so this is a bit redundant.

As I said in the readability section, the reality check is not convincing. The student treats the fact that they have 42,412 observations in the cleaned dataset just as Kuppermann et al. do as a sign of consistency, but this is to be expected since both the student and Kuppermann et al. took the exact same steps in filtering observations: getting rid of those with missing outcome labels (ciTBI) and those with GCS scores of 3-13, so of course both of them end up with the same 42,412 observations.

Yes, using bootstrapping of the cohort to see if logistic regression still yields similar deciles makes sense to me, although they didn't do a stability check on the capture/lift curve, which is also part of Finding 1. I don't quite understand the decile curves, but the fact that D9 contains the line in Finding 1 but not in the bootstrap resample makes me a bit suspicious of the stability of the result.
